messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan's life was forever changed when his older brother, Kumar, died suddenly in a car accident six months ago. Rohan had always looked up to Kumar, who was not only his sibling but also his closest friend and confidant. The two brothers shared a love for writing and would often spend hours discussing literature and working on their own stories together. After the funeral, Rohan found himself unable to relax even in the safety of his own home, constantly jumping at ordinary sounds like creaks and groans that he had never noticed before. As time passed, Rohan became increasingly convinced that the world was a dangerous place where tragedy could strike at any moment. He started to believe that his own happiness was lost forever, replaced by an unshakeable sense of misery. These thoughts only intensified his fear of making plans for the future, which now seemed precarious and uncertain. "What's the point of planning anything," Rohan would ask himself, "when everything can be taken away in an instant?" This fear led him to avoid thinking about or discussing any long-term goals or aspirations with others. Rohan's friends and family tried to reassure him that he was okay, but he found himself constantly seeking reassurance from them. He would call his parents multiple times a day, asking if they were safe, and text his friends excessively, needing to know that they were all right. This behavior only served to reinforce Rohan's negative appraisals of the world, as he began to see himself as someone who was too fragile to cope with life's uncertainties. As Rohan struggled to come to terms with his loss, he found it increasingly difficult to focus on his writing, a passion that had once brought him so much joy. He would sit at his desk, staring blankly at the page, unable to shake off the feeling of impending doom that seemed to hover over him like a dark cloud. The silence was oppressive, punctuated only by the occasional startle response when a bird chirped or a car drove by outside. Sleep became another casualty of Rohan's newfound fears. He would lie awake at night, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios and catastrophic thoughts. His parents tried to help him establish a bedtime routine, but nothing seemed to work. The exhaustion only added to Rohan's sense of hopelessness, making it even more challenging for him to confront the world outside. As the months dragged on, Rohan became increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings and events that might remind him of Kumar or trigger painful memories. He stopped attending writing workshops and meetings with fellow writers, afraid of being asked about his work or sharing his stories. This withdrawal only served to reinforce Rohan's negative appraisals of himself and the world around him. One day, while browsing through old family photos, Rohan stumbled upon a picture of him and Kumar taken on a camping trip a few years ago. The memories came flooding back, and for a moment, he felt like he was drowning in grief all over again. It was then that Rohan realized he couldn't keep living like this – constantly on edge, afraid to face the future or engage with the world around him. He knew he needed help, not just to cope with his loss but also to rebuild his shattered sense of self and the world. With a newfound determination, Rohan picked up the phone and made an appointment with a therapist, hoping that she could guide him through this dark tunnel and back into the light.
